fetched_contents.text: Effects of Soil Compaction Introduction The threat of soil compaction is greater today than in the past because of the dramatic increase in the size of farm equipment (Figure 1). Therefore, producers must pay more attention to soil compaction than they have in the past. In this fact sheet we will discuss the effects of soil compaction and briefly identify ways to avoid or alleviate it. Effects of Compaction on Crop Yields Soil Compaction Effects on Forages The effect of traffic on alfalfa and grass sod is a combination of soil compaction and stand damage. In a recent study in Wisconsin and Iowa, annual alfalfa yield losses up to 37 percent due to normal field traffic were recorded. Based on this work, a multistate project was initiated to get a better understanding of yield losses due to traffic in alfalfa. Yield losses ranged from 1 to 34 percent (Figure 2). The damage to alfalfa stands is much greater 5 days after cutting than 2 days after cutting, showing the importance of timeliness in removing silage or hay from the field. Soil Compaction Effects on Tilled Soils Tillage is often performed to remove ruts, and farmers assume that it takes care of soil compaction. Thus, farmers become careless and disregard soil moisture conditions for traffic and other important principles of soil compaction avoidance, assuming that they can always correct the problem with tillage. Distinguishing between topsoil and subsoil compaction is important. Research has shown that tillage can alleviate effects of topsoil compaction on sandy soils in 1 year. However, on heavier soils more tillage passes and repeated freeze-dry cycles are required to alleviate effects of surface compaction. Therefore, the effects of topsoil compaction reduce yields on these soils despite tillage. Since most soils in Pennsylvania contain significant amounts of clay in their surface horizons, topsoil compaction is likely to reduce crop yields, even with tillage. Subsoil compaction is below the depth of normal tillage operations. Research shows that subsoil compaction is not alleviated by freeze-thaw and wetting-drying cycles on any soil type. In an international research effort that included tillage after compaction, average first-year yield losses were approximately 15 percent, although results varied from year to year and from site to site (Figure 3). This first-year loss was considered to be primarily the result of topsoil compaction residual effects. Without recompaction, yield losses decreased to approximately 3 percent 10 years after the compaction event. The final yield loss, which was most likely due to subsoil compaction, can be considered permanent. The effects of subsoil compaction are due to using high axle loads (10 tons and heavier) on wet soil and are observed in all types of soils (including sandy soils). Tillage can also cause the formation of a tillage pan. The most damaging form of tillage is moldboard plowing with one wheel (or horse) in the furrow, which causes direct subsoil compaction. On-land moldboard plowing is certainly preferred over this practice. However, even then the moldboard plow can still cause compaction just below the plow. The disk is another implement that can cause the formation of such a pan. In our research in Pennsylvania, we also observed the formation of plow pans on dairy farms that used the chisel plow (Figure 4). More tillage operations and more power are needed to prepare a seedbed in compacted soil. This leads to increased pulverization of the soil and a general deterioration of soil structure, which makes the soil more sensitive to recompaction. Therefore, compaction can enforce a vicious tillage spiral that degrades soil (Figure 5) and results in increased emissions of the greenhouse gases carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide due to increased fuel consumption and slower water percolation. Ammonia losses also increase because of decreased infiltration in compacted soil. More runoff will cause increased erosion and nutrient and pesticide losses to surface waters. At the same time, reduced percolation through the soil profile restricts the potential for groundwater recharge from compacted soils. Thus, this vicious compaction/tillage spiral is an environmental threat with impacts beyond the individual field. Soil Compaction Effects on No-Till Crop Production No-till has a lot of advantages over tillage--reduced labor requirements, reduced equipment costs, less runoff and erosion, increased drought resistance of crops, and higher organic matter content and biological activity. The higher organic matter content and biological activity in no-till makes the soil more resilient to soil compaction. One study illustrates this very well (Figure 6). Topsoil from long-term no-till and conventional till fields were subject to a standard compaction treatment at different moisture contents. The "Proctor Density Test" is used to determine what the maximum compactability of soil is. The conventional till soil could be compacted to a maximum density of 1.65 g/cm3, which is considered root limiting for this soil. The no-till soil could only be compacted to 1.40 g/cm3, which is not considered root limiting. Thus, topsoil compaction would be less of a concern in no-till fields. The increased firmness of no-till soils makes them more accessible, and no-till fields may become better drained over time. This being said, compaction can still have significant negative effects on the productivity of no-till soils. fetched_contents.text: Soil compaction and the architectural plasticity of root systems ---------------------------------------- We present examples of root plasticity in response to soil compaction and discuss their role in plant performance. Subsequently, we propose a plastic ideotype for soil compaction tolerance. Keywords: Adaptive plasticity, enotype×environment interaction, phenotypic variation, root responses, root traits, soil bulk density, soil strength Abstract Soil compaction is a serious global problem, and is a major cause of inadequate rooting and poor yield in crops around the world. Root system architecture (RSA) describes the spatial arrangement of root components within the soil and determines the plant’s exploration of the soil. Soil strength restricts root growth and may slow down root system development. RSA plasticity may have an adaptive value, providing environmental tolerance to soil compaction. However, it is challenging to distinguish developmental retardation (apparent plasticity) or responses to severe stress from those root architectural changes that may provide an actual environmental tolerance (adaptive plasticity). In this review, we outline the consequences of soil compaction on the rooting environment and extensively review the various root responses reported in the literature. Finally, we discuss which responses enhance root exploration capabilities in tolerant genotypes, and to what extent these responses might be useful for breeding. We conclude that RSA plasticity in response to soil compaction is complex and can be targeted in breeding to increase the performance of crops under specific agronomical conditions. Introduction Plant root functions are: soil water and nutrient uptake, anchorage, reserve storage, vegetative propagation (e.g. Weaver, 1926; Fitter, 1987), and root to shoot signaling (Shabala et al., 2015). Root system architecture (RSA) describes the spatial arrangement of root components within the soil [i.e. the spatial arrangement of nodal, lateral (first-, second-, ith-order), primary roots, etc.]. RSA determines the plant’s exploration of the soil to forage for water and nutrients (e.g. Lynch, 1995, 2007b). RSA results from three processes: extending root tips, formation of lateral roots, and tropisms or curvatures (e.g. Lynch, 1995; Smith and De Smet, 2012; Rogers and Benfey, 2015). These processes respond dynamically to soil bio-physico-chemical properties that vary in time and space, and therefore the resulting RSA phenotype arises from both the plant genetics and the soil conditions. This responsiveness of RSA to soil conditions can be termed ‘RSA plasticity’. An individual organism cannot be considered outside the context of its environment (Bradshaw, 1965), and the actual phenotype of a particular genotype depends on the particular environment that it experiences (Via et al., 1995). In a broad sense, phenotypic plasticity is the property of a given genotype to express different phenotypes under different environmental conditions (Bradshaw, 1965; Sultan, 1987; Via et al., 1995; Pigliucci, 2001; Palmer et al., 2012). Phenotypic plasticity is thought to enable plants to cope with or even take advantage of environmental heterogeneity (Crossett et al., 1975; Via et al., 1995; Forde, 2002; El-Soda et al., 2014). Although plasticity can provide an increased environmental tolerance in many circumstances (Bradshaw, 1965; Via et al., 1995; Palmer et al., 2012; Des Marais et al., 2013), this is not always the case. If plasticity is expressed, it may not have any appreciable, beneficial effect, and it may even be counterproductive (see below). Here we review the literature to establish the importance of RSA plasticity in the context of soil strength. Soil strength is a major cause of inadequate rooting. It affects nearly all soil bio-physico-chemical properties (Håkansson et al., 1988) such as soil porosity, water conductivity, and nutrient availability, and millions of hectares of agricultural lands are affected globally (Oldeman et al., 1991). While the majority of affected lands are located in Europe, Africa, and Asia, some areas of the Americas are also prone to compaction (Soane and van Ouwerkerk, 1994). Yield losses by compaction have been estimated to be ~20% (Arvidsson, 1999) and 25% (Barken et al., 1987). Higher estimates (~50–75%) occur when the soil is affected by another constraint such as drought (Hoque and Kobata, 2000). In Fig. 1, we compiled an overview of the negative effect of soil compaction on yield in several crops, soils, and countries. The lower yields result from reduced uptake of water and nutrients, and lower biomass, which in turn are consequences of soil mechanical impedance on root growth and development (Håkansson et al., 1988; Lipiec and Stępniewski, 1995; Stirzaker et al., 1996; Passioura, 2002). In this review, we do not discuss the effect of soil compaction on the soil microbiota and their interactions with the roots and surrounding rhizosphere because it is a complex topic. Nevertheless, mechanical impedance can increase the accumulation of microorganisms on roots, making the plant more prone to infection and disease (Watt et al., 2003). As far as we know, the role of RSA plasticity in providing tolerance to soil compaction is poorly understood. Few studies have addressed RSA plasticity directly and, additionally, it is challenging to distinguish adaptive mechanisms from ontological processes. fetched_contents.text: Effect of soil compaction on photosynthesis and carbon partitioning within a maize–soil system Abstract Soil compaction is known to affect plant growth. However, most of the information regarding the effects of this factor on carbon partitioning has been obtained on young plants while little is known about the evolution of these effects with plant age. The objective of this work was to investigate how soil compaction affects carbon assimilation, photosynthate partitioning and morphology of maize plants during vegetative growth up to tassel initiation. A pressure was applied on moist soil to obtain a bulk density of 1.45 g cm−3 (compacted soil (CS) treatment) while the loose soil (LS) treatment (bulk density of 1.30 g cm−3) was obtained by gentle vibration of soil columns. Plants were grown in a growth chamber for 3–6 weeks and carbon partitioning in the plant–soil system was evaluated using 14C pulse-labelling techniques. Soil compaction greatly hampered root elongation and delayed leaf appearance rate, thereby decreasing plant height, shoot and root dry weights and leaf area. The increase in soil bulk density decreased carbon assimilation rate especially in early growth stages. The main effect of soil compaction on assimilate partitioning occurred on carbon exudation, which increased considerably to the detriment of root carbon. Furthermore, soil microbial biomass greatly increased in CS. Two hypotheses were formulated. The first was that increasing soil resistance to root penetration induced a sink limitation in roots and this increased carbon release into the soil and resulted in a root feedback that regulated carbon assimilation rate. The second hypothesis relies on soil–plant water relations since, due to compaction, the pore size distribution has to be considered. In a compacted soil, the peak of the pore size distribution curve is shifted towards the small pore size. The volume of small pores increases and the unsaturated conductivity decreases substantially, when compared to non-compacted soil. Due to small hydraulic conductivity, the inflow into the roots is well below optimum and the plant closes stomata thus reducing carbon assimilation rate. The effects of soil compaction persisted with plant age although the difference between the two treatments, in terms of percentage, decreased at advanced growth stages, especially in the case of root parameters. This constraint results in restricted root growth that in turn may affect the whole plant growth and grain yield (Canarache et al., 1984). The most pronounced effect of soil compaction is the reduction of root length. Several authors have observed such an effect under different growth conditions. Logsdon et al. (1987) indicated that increasing soil bulk density caused a linear decrease in maize root length with the increase in soil bulk density. Similar results were obtained with different crops (maize, barley, wheat, peas and beans) and various culture media (soil and nutrient solution with glass beads) (Abdalla et al., 1969, Asady and Smucker, 1989, Kayombo et al., 1991, Grath and Hakansson, 1992, Oussible et al., 1992, Groleau-Renaud et al., 1998). Meanwhile, the effect of soil compaction on root biomass depends on compactness degree, soil water status, and soil physical properties. For instance, while Atwell (1990a) observed that soil compaction increased root biomass of wheat, other authors have shown that increasing compactive stress decreases root dry weight of maize (Panayiotopoulos et al., 1994). These morphological modifications probably affect water and nutrient uptake. Soil compaction effects extend beyond root morphology, affecting both shoot morphology and general plant physiology. A reduction in leaf area and shoot biomass was observed in maize plants grown on compacted soil (Ekwue and Stone, 1995). Furthermore, several authors have reported a decrease in photosynthetic activity due to a drop in stomatal conductance in plants grown on compacted soils (Masle et al., 1990, Tardieu et al., 1992). This decrease was attributed to a chemical message, mainly abscisic acid (ABA), produced in the stressed roots and travelling to shoots via the xylem sap (Masle et al., 1990, Tardieu, 1994). Carbon partitioning within the maize–soil system was the subject of several papers (Liljeroth et al., 1994, Qian et al., 1997). However, the effect of soil compaction on carbon partitioning has rarely been investigated. Studying carbon partitioning under different bulk densities is of major interest as it determines root:shoot ratio and grain yield. Sauerbeck and Helal (1986) labelled maize plants continuously from day 7 to day 23 in order to study photosynthate distribution. They reported increases with increasing soil bulk density in both the fraction of carbon recovered in the soil and in that respired by roots and soil microorganisms. On the other hand, 14C remaining in roots decreased with increasing soil strength. Similarly, root exudation was stimulated when roots of young maize plants were impeded in a glass bead nutrient solution (Boeuf-Tremblay et al., 1995). A main shortage in existing data is that they were obtained using very young plants (up to 3 weeks old). Moreover, some of the previous works were conducted in hydroponic conditions that do not represent soil conditions. The aim of the present paper is to track the evolution of the effects of soil compaction on photosynthesis, carbon partitioning (including in the rhizosphere) and plant morphology of maize plants ageing from 21 to 42 days (shortly before tassel initiation). fetched_contents.text: A meta-analysis of the impact of traffic-induced compaction on soil physical properties and grain yield Highlights * • Compaction increased soil mechanical strength, particularly in the topsoil. * • Compaction decreased air and water transport down to the subsoil. * • Soil compaction decreased grain yield of corn, wheat, barley and soybean by 6 and up to 34%. * • Abstract Soil compaction caused by wheel traffic is a major driver of soil degradation in modern agriculture and thus, a threat to agricultural sustainability. To improve the predictive capacity of compaction models and to support decision-making that implements site-specific practices for ameliorating soil compaction effects in modern agriculture, we need quantitative syntheses of the effect of soil compaction on soil physical properties and crop types. In this work, we used a meta-analytical approach to summarize results from 51 published articles on the impacts of soil compaction attributed to machinery axle load, wheel passes, compaction events and tire inflation pressure on soil bulk density (ρb), degree of compactness (DC), penetration resistance (PR), volume of water filled pores at field capacity (θFc), air permeability (ka) at field capacity, saturated hydraulic conductivity (ksat), and grain yield of corn (Zea mays L.), wheat (Triticum aestivum L.), barley (Hordeum vulgare L.) and soybean (Glycine max L.). Results from this meta-analysis (MA) showed that compaction increased soil mechanical strength shown by increased soil ρb, DC and PR. However, an increase in soil strength was more pronounced in the medium- and coarse-textured soils, and mainly in the topsoil (0–30 cm depth). Penetration resistance for the non-compacted soil (control) treatment was 1.21 MPa for the coarse-textured, 1.11 MPa for the medium-textured and 0.93 MPa for the fine-textured soils. Soil compaction on average, increased PR by 99, 94 and by 41 percent in the medium-, coarse- and fine-textured soils. Compaction decreased hydraulic conductivity characterized by ka and ksat from the topsoil down to the subsoil (>40 cm depth), and grain yield of corn, wheat, barley, and soybean. Overall, compaction decreased grain yield on average by 6–34 percent. Findings of the MA suggest that soil hydraulic properties may be more sensitive indicators to reflect the impact of soil compaction on soil structure and pore system functions in the soil profile. Future efforts should place a greater emphasis on the publication of complete metadata that allows replication and accurate comparison of results across studies and on providing open access to original datasets that can be used to improve our understanding of the effect of traffic-induced compaction on soil functioning, including crop production. Field traffic, particularly in wet condition can cause soil compaction, defined as the densification and reduction in soil porosity, which alters soil structure, increases soil strength, and reduces soil hydraulic conductivity (Soane and van Ouwerkerk, 1994). Susceptibility of agricultural soils to topsoil and subsoil compaction has increased over the past decades due to a steady increase in wheel load of agricultural machinery (Keller et al., 2019). In general, three regions of compaction could be identified throughout the soil profile, namely topsoil or surface compaction, upper subsoil compaction, and subsoil or deep soil compaction, i.e., compaction beyond the normal tilled zone (Abu-Hamdeh, 2003). The topsoil is the uppermost soil layer, generally comprising the top ∼30 cm in depth. For agricultural soils, the upper subsoil refers to the layer from approximately 30–40 cm depth. In no-tilled soils, the depth of the upper subsoil and deep soil compaction is defined as the layers less affected by natural compaction alleviating processes such as freezing and thawing and the activities of soil biota (Schjønning et al., 2015). As compaction deforms soil structure, reduces porosity and alters pore morphology, it has cascading negative effects on water storage and transport, root growth and nutrient availability (Keller et al., 2017; Schjønning et al., 2017). These changes in turn negatively affect food production, habitat for soil organisms, and several other ecosystem functions (e.g., regulation of climate and water provision and purification) (Batey, 2009; Berisso et al., 2013). Compaction increases soil mechanical strength, which can be quantified in terms of soil bulk density (ρb) and penetration resistance (PR). Soil compaction alters root development by reducing root penetration and increasing soil resistance, with evidence from multiple sources converging on these mechanisms. The physical effects of compaction are directly linked to increased bulk density, reduced porosity, and decreased macropore space, which makes it harder for roots to move through the soil profile and reduces water and air movement [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R5][N1-F1]. Compaction also increases soil mechanical strength, as indicated by higher bulk density, degree of compactness, and penetration resistance, which are measures of resistance to root growth [N4-F4]. In compacted soils, roots face greater impedance, which can delay emergence, impede root growth and proliferation, and limit water and nutrient uptake [N4-F4][N1-F1].

On root elongation, branching, and lateral root formation, the evidence shows that soil compaction restricts root growth and can reduce root length. A meta-analysis found that compaction decreased grain yield and that higher soil strength was associated with reduced root growth and proliferation [N4-F4]. The root plasticity review also notes that soil strength restricts root growth and may slow root system development, while root system architecture (RSA) plasticity can include responses such as shortened root length, increased root diameter, and fewer lateral roots [N2-F2]. The review further argues that RSA plasticity is a major response to soil compaction and can be targeted in breeding for improved tolerance [N2-F2]. Another source explicitly states that soil compaction reduces root elongation and delays leaf appearance rate, which in turn reduces shoot and root dry weights and leaf area [N3-F3]. In compacted soil, root growth is constrained not just by resistance but also by altered pore structure, which shifts the pore size distribution toward smaller pores and reduces unsaturated conductivity [N3-F3].

The evidence also shows that compaction affects root distribution depth and access to water and nutrients. Compaction reduces rooting depth and increases the resistance to root penetration, which limits the ability of roots to explore soil resources [N2-F2][N1-F1]. In maize, compaction reduced root length and delayed root elongation, while also reducing root dry weight [N3-F3]. Because compaction decreases porosity and alters pore morphology, it can reduce water storage and transport, which in turn limits root access to water and nutrients [N4-F4][N1-F1]. The meta-analysis emphasizes that compaction decreases hydraulic conductivity and reduces soil hydraulic properties such as air permeability and saturated hydraulic conductivity, which are critical for water movement through the soil profile [N4-F4]. Compacted soils are therefore less able to supply water and nutrients efficiently to the root system, which is a major constraint on root function [N4-F4].

Taken together, the evidence supports a consistent picture: soil compaction increases mechanical impedance, reduces root penetration, and alters root morphology by decreasing elongation, branching, and lateral root formation. It also restricts root depth and access to water and nutrients by reducing porosity, pore size distribution, and hydraulic conductivity [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R5][N4-F4][N2-F2][N3-F3].

Soil compaction indirectly affects shoot development by constraining root growth and altering the physiological environment that roots transmit signals to shoots. The evidence shows that root constraints reduce the volume of soil explored by the root system, which limits the supply of water and nutrients to shoots and thus limits shoot growth [N3-R2]. In maize, soil compaction greatly hampered root elongation and delayed leaf appearance rate, thereby decreasing plant height, shoot and root dry weights, and leaf area [N3-F3]. The same source also notes that reduced leaf area and shoot biomass were observed in maize grown on compacted soil [N3-F3]. Compaction can therefore reduce shoot growth by reducing the plant’s ability to acquire resources through the root system [N3-R2][N3-F3].

Changes in canopy development, leaf area, and tillering are also evident. The maize study found that compaction reduced leaf area and shoot biomass [N3-F3], while the broader compaction literature indicates that shoot growth is closely tied to root exploration and resource supply [N3-R2]. The review on root system architecture states that RSA determines the plant’s exploration of the soil to forage for water and nutrients and that reduced rooting can lower biomass and yield [N2-F2]. In compacted soils, the plant may also experience physiological stress signals that limit shoot development. The maize study reports that soil compaction decreased carbon assimilation rate, particularly in early growth stages, and that this was linked to reduced stomatal conductance and a drop in photosynthetic activity [N3-F3]. It also notes that a chemical message, mainly abscisic acid (ABA), produced in stressed roots and traveling via xylem sap to shoots, can reduce carbon assimilation rate [N3-F3]. This indicates a direct physiological link between root stress and shoot physiology.

The evidence also suggests that shoot responses are not uniform across all growth stages or management contexts. In the maize study, the effects of compaction persisted with plant age, although the percentage differences decreased at advanced growth stages, especially for root parameters [N3-F3]. This implies that shoot responses can be partly buffered over time, but the underlying root constraints remain a limiting factor. The long-term compaction evidence adds that yield losses can be short-term or long-term, with topsoil compaction often having a more immediate yield impact and subsoil compaction being harder to recover [N6-F2][N6-F5]. In long-term studies, yield loss can decrease over time, but subsoil compaction may have a more permanent effect [N1-F1][N6-F5].

Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that soil compaction indirectly reduces shoot growth by restricting root exploration, reducing water and nutrient supply, and triggering physiological stress signals that lower carbon assimilation and photosynthetic activity [N3-R2][N3-F3][N2-F2]. The shoot response includes reduced leaf area, reduced shoot biomass, and reduced canopy development, with these effects mediated through root constraints and root-to-shoot signaling [N3-F3][N3-R2].

The evidence on compaction effects on crop yield is substantial and consistent across major crops and soils. A meta-analysis found that soil compaction decreased grain yield of corn, wheat, barley, and soybean by 6–34% on average, with compaction also increasing soil mechanical strength and reducing hydraulic conductivity [N4-F4]. The same source reports that compaction decreased air and water transport down to the subsoil, which is an important mechanism linking compaction to yield loss [N4-F4]. Other evidence shows that compaction can cause large yield losses in specific crops and situations, including up to 37% in annual alfalfa, with losses ranging from 1 to 34% in a multistate project [N1-F1]. This indicates that yield reductions are not confined to one crop or one soil type; they are observed across major crops and soils [N1-F1][N4-F4].

The evidence also distinguishes between short-term and long-term effects of compaction. In the meta-analysis, compaction-induced yield losses persisted over time, but the magnitude of the loss can decline with age [N4-F4]. The Pennsylvania study notes that yield losses from topsoil compaction were often reduced over time, while subsoil compaction can have more permanent effects [N1-F1]. Specifically, in some cases yield losses decreased from about 15% in the first year to about 3% 10 years after compaction, with the final yield loss likely due to subsoil compaction [N1-F1]. In a long-term no-till study, compacted soil had a dramatic first-year effect on corn yield, with yield only 2% of uncompacted soil, but the yields recovered to 85% the second year and stabilized after that [N1-F1]. This shows that compaction can have both acute and delayed yield impacts, with some recovery possible over time depending on the type of compaction and management [N1-F1][N4-F4].

Management practices play a key role in mitigating yield loss. Conservation tillage is highlighted as a long-term solution, because it avoids tillage passes and preserves soil structure [N6-R3]. The meta-analysis also notes that soil hydraulic properties may be more sensitive indicators of compaction effects than bulk density alone, suggesting that management should target soil structure and water movement rather than only bulk density [N4-F4]. The evidence also shows that no-till soils can be less vulnerable to topsoil compaction because they are less easily compacted and may remain more accessible [N1-F1]. However, compaction can still have significant negative effects on no-till soils, as shown by a 30-bushel yield decrease in a dry year and a 20-bushel yield loss in a wet year [N1-F1]. This indicates that management practices can reduce yield loss, but they cannot fully eliminate it in all circumstances [N1-F1][N4-F4].

Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that soil compaction reduces crop yield across major crops and soils, with yield reductions ranging from about 6% to over 34% on average [N4-F4][N1-F1]. Short-term effects are often more pronounced, especially when compaction occurs in topsoil, while long-term effects can persist or become permanent if subsoil compaction develops [N1-F1][N4-F4]. Management practices such as conservation tillage, no-till, and attention to soil moisture and traffic timing can help mitigate yield loss, but the effectiveness of these practices depends on soil type, compaction depth, and the specific crop [N1-F1][N6-R3][N4-F4].

Root-soil hydraulic coupling mediates compaction effects on water and nutrient uptake by linking root hydraulic properties to soil hydraulic conductivity and water availability. The evidence shows that root hydraulic properties are key physiological traits that determine the capacity of root systems to take up water at a given evaporative demand [N7-R5]. During soil drying, the drop in soil–plant hydraulic conductance causes a decline in root water uptake, which is impacted by both soil and root hydraulic phenotypes [N7-R1]. This indicates that root water uptake is not only limited by soil structure but also by the plant’s ability to transport water from the soil to the shoot [N7-R1][N7-R5].

Compaction affects soil hydraulic conductivity and water availability by reducing hydraulic conductivity and altering pore structure. The meta-analysis found that compaction decreased hydraulic conductivity characterized by air permeability and saturated hydraulic conductivity, and that this effect extended down to the subsoil [N4-F4]. Compaction also shifts pore size distribution toward smaller pores and reduces unsaturated conductivity, which reduces the inflow into roots and can cause the plant to close stomata [N3-F3]. This creates a feedback loop in which reduced hydraulic conductivity limits water uptake, reducing stomatal conductance and carbon assimilation rate [N3-F3]. The evidence also notes that soil water retention and transport properties are altered in response to compaction, which affects soil water flow [N7-R4]. Overall, compaction reduces water availability by decreasing hydraulic conductivity, reducing pore size distribution, and altering the soil’s ability to transmit water to roots [N4-F4][N3-F3][N7-R4].

Nutrient uptake is constrained by water transport limitations because water movement is a prerequisite for nutrient uptake and for maintaining root function. The maize study found that compaction reduced root elongation and delayed leaf appearance rate, thereby decreasing shoot and root dry weights and leaf area, and that carbon assimilation was reduced in early growth stages [N3-F3]. It also notes that reduced leaf area and shoot biomass were observed in maize grown on compacted soil, and that reduced photosynthetic activity was attributed to a drop in stomatal conductance and a chemical message from stressed roots [N3-F3]. This shows that nutrient and carbon acquisition are not independent of water uptake: reduced water availability can limit stomatal opening, reduce photosynthesis, and ultimately reduce the plant’s ability to assimilate and partition carbon [N3-F3]. The meta-analysis further states that changes in soil pore structure and hydraulic properties can negatively affect water storage and transport, root growth, and nutrient availability [N4-F4].

Taken together, the evidence supports the conclusion that root-soil hydraulic coupling is central to compaction effects on water and nutrient uptake. Compaction reduces hydraulic conductivity and water availability by altering pore structure, decreasing unsaturated conductivity, and reducing the inflow into roots [N3-F3][N4-F4][N7-R4]. It also constrains nutrient uptake because water transport limitations can reduce stomatal conductance, carbon assimilation, and overall plant function [N3-F3][N7-R1]. Root hydraulic properties determine how effectively the root system can uptake water, which means that compaction affects nutrient acquisition through its impact on both soil hydraulic conditions and root hydraulic capacity [N7-R5][N7-R1][N3-F3].

Soil compaction influences crop yield through a cascade of effects on root development, shoot development, and the physiological mechanisms that connect them. The evidence from the branch reports shows that compaction reduces root penetration and increases resistance, changes root elongation, branching, and lateral root formation, and alters root distribution depth and access to water and nutrients. Compaction restricts root growth and can reduce root length. Root-soil hydraulic coupling mediates compaction effects on water and nutrient uptake by linking root hydraulic properties to soil hydraulic conductivity and water availability. Soil compaction begins with increased bulk density, reduced porosity, and decreased macropore space, which make it harder for roots to move through the soil profile [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R5][N1-F1]. The physical evidence is consistent across sources: compaction reduces porosity, alters pore morphology, and increases resistance to root penetration [N1-F1][N4-F4].

Compaction restricts root growth and can reduce root length. A meta-analysis found that compaction decreased grain yield and that higher soil strength was associated with reduced root growth and proliferation [N4-F4]. The root plasticity review notes that soil strength restricts root growth and may slow root system development, while root system architecture (RSA) plasticity can include responses such as shortened root length, increased root diameter, and fewer lateral roots [N2-F2]. In maize, compaction greatly hampered root elongation and delayed leaf appearance rate, thereby reducing shoot and root dry weights and leaf area [N3-F3]. This indicates that compaction not only reduces root length but also alters root morphology and branching patterns.

Compaction reduces rooting depth and increases resistance to root penetration, which limits the ability of roots to explore soil resources [N2-F2][N1-F1]. In maize, compaction reduced root length and delayed root elongation, while also reducing root dry weight [N3-F3]. Because compaction decreases porosity and alters pore morphology, it can reduce water storage and transport, which in turn limits root access to water and nutrients [N4-F4][N1-F1]. The meta-analysis emphasizes that compaction decreases hydraulic conductivity and reduces soil hydraulic properties such as air permeability and saturated hydraulic conductivity, which are critical for water movement through the soil profile [N4-F4]. Compacted soils are therefore less able to supply water and nutrients efficiently to the root system, which is a major constraint on root function [N4-F4].

## 4) Compaction indirectly affects shoot development
Soil compaction indirectly affects shoot development by constraining root growth and altering the physiological environment that roots transmit signals to shoots. The evidence also suggests that shoot responses include changes in canopy development, leaf area, and tillering. The maize study found that compaction reduced leaf area and shoot biomass [N3-F3]. ## 2) Compaction changes root elongation, branching, and lateral root formation
Compaction restricts root growth and can reduce root length. A meta-analysis found that compaction decreased grain yield and that higher soil strength was associated with reduced root growth and proliferation [N4-F4]. The root plasticity review notes that soil strength restricts root growth and may slow root system development, while root system architecture (RSA) plasticity can include responses such as shortened root length, increased root diameter, and fewer lateral roots [N2-F2]. In maize, compaction greatly hampered root elongation and delayed leaf appearance rate, thereby reducing shoot and root dry weights and leaf area [N3-F3]. This indicates that compaction not only reduces root length but also alters root morphology and branching patterns.

## 3) Compaction affects root distribution depth and access to water/nutrients
Compaction reduces rooting depth and increases resistance to root penetration, which limits the ability of roots to explore soil resources [N2-F2][N1-F1]. In maize, compaction reduced root length and delayed root elongation, while also reducing root dry weight [N3-F3]. Because compaction decreases porosity and alters pore morphology, it can reduce water storage and transport, which in turn limits root access to water and nutrients [N4-F4][N1-F1]. The meta-analysis emphasizes that compaction decreases hydraulic conductivity and reduces soil hydraulic properties such as air permeability and saturated hydraulic conductivity, which are critical for water movement through the soil profile [N4-F4]. Compacted soils are therefore less able to supply water and nutrients efficiently to the root system, which is a major constraint on root function [N4-F4].

## 4) Compaction indirectly affects shoot development
Soil compaction indirectly affects shoot development by constraining root growth and altering the physiological environment that roots transmit signals to shoots. The evidence shows that root constraints reduce the volume of soil explored by the root system, which limits the supply of water and nutrients to shoots and thus limits shoot growth [N3-R2]. In maize, soil compaction greatly hampered root elongation and delayed leaf appearance rate, thereby decreasing plant height, shoot and root dry weights, and leaf area [N3-F3]. The same source also notes that reduced leaf area and shoot biomass were observed in maize grown on compacted soil [N3-F3]. Compaction can therefore reduce shoot growth by reducing the plant’s ability to acquire resources through the root system [N3-R2][N3-F3].

## 5) Changes in canopy development, leaf area, and tillering
The evidence also suggests that shoot responses include changes in canopy development, leaf area, and tillering. The maize study found that compaction reduced leaf area and shoot biomass [N3-F3]. The broader compaction literature indicates that shoot growth is closely tied to root exploration and resource supply [N3-R2]. Compaction can also affect tillering indirectly, because reduced root resources and altered plant physiology can constrain overall plant growth and the ability to form additional shoots [N3-F3]. The review on root system architecture states that RSA determines the plant’s exploration of the soil to forage for water and nutrients and that reduced rooting can lower biomass and yield [N2-F2].

## 6) Physiological stress signals linking roots to shoots
Compaction can trigger physiological stress signals that link roots to shoots. The maize study reports that soil compaction decreased carbon assimilation rate, particularly in early growth stages, and that this was linked to reduced stomatal conductance and a drop in photosynthetic activity [N3-F3]. It also notes that a chemical message, mainly abscisic acid (ABA), produced in stressed roots and traveling via xylem sap to shoots, can reduce carbon assimilation rate [N3-F3]. This indicates a direct physiological link between root stress and shoot physiology. The evidence supports the idea that root constraints can induce shoot-level changes through hormonal and transport signals rather than only through direct resource limitation [N3-F3][N2-F2].

## 7) Short-term vs long-term effects on crop yield
The evidence on crop yield shows that compaction reduces yield across major crops and soils, with yield reductions ranging from about 6% to over 34% on average [N4-F4][N1-F1]. The meta-analysis found that soil compaction decreased grain yield of corn, wheat, barley, and soybean by 6–34% on average, with compaction also increasing soil mechanical strength and reducing hydraulic conductivity [N4-F4]. Other evidence shows that compaction can cause large yield losses in specific crops and situations, including up to 37% in annual alfalfa, with losses ranging from 1 to 34% in a multistate project [N1-F1]. This indicates that yield reductions are not confined to one crop or one soil type; they are observed across major crops and soils [N1-F1][N4-F4].

The evidence also distinguishes between short-term and long-term effects of compaction. In the meta-analysis, compaction-induced yield losses persisted over time, but the magnitude of the loss can decline with age [N4-F4]. The Pennsylvania study notes that yield losses from topsoil compaction were often reduced over time, while subsoil compaction can have more permanent effects [N1-F1]. Specifically, in some cases yield losses decreased from about 15% in the first year to about 3% 10 years after compaction, with the final yield loss likely due to subsoil compaction [N1-F1]. In a long-term no-till study, compacted soil had a dramatic first-year effect on corn yield, with yield only 2% of uncompacted soil, but the yields recovered to 85% the second year and stabilized after that [N1-F1]. This shows that compaction can have both acute and delayed yield impacts, with some recovery possible over time depending on the type of compaction and management [N1-F1][N4-F4].

## 8) Role of management practices in mitigating yield loss
Management practices play a key role in mitigating yield loss. Conservation tillage is highlighted as a long-term solution, because it avoids tillage passes and preserves soil structure [N6-R3]. The meta-analysis also notes that soil hydraulic properties may be more sensitive indicators of compaction effects than bulk density alone, suggesting that management should target soil structure and water movement rather than only bulk density [N4-F4]. The evidence also shows that no-till soils can be less vulnerable to topsoil compaction because they are less easily compacted and may remain more accessible [N1-F1]. However, compaction can still have significant negative effects on no-till soils, as shown by a 30-bushel yield decrease in a dry year and a 20-bushel yield loss in a wet year [N1-F1]. This indicates that management practices can reduce yield loss, but they cannot fully eliminate it in all circumstances [N1-F1][N4-F4].

## 9) Root-soil hydraulic coupling and nutrient uptake
Root-soil hydraulic coupling mediates compaction effects on water and nutrient uptake by linking root hydraulic properties to soil hydraulic conductivity and water availability. The evidence shows that root hydraulic properties are key physiological traits that determine the capacity of root systems to take up water at a given evaporative demand [N7-R5]. During soil drying, the drop in soil–plant hydraulic conductance causes a decline in root water uptake, which is impacted by both soil and root hydraulic phenotypes [N7-R1]. This indicates that root water uptake is not only limited by soil structure but also by the plant’s ability to transport water from the soil to the shoot [N7-R1][N7-R5].

Compaction affects soil hydraulic conductivity and water availability by reducing hydraulic conductivity and altering pore structure. The meta-analysis found that compaction decreased hydraulic conductivity characterized by air permeability and saturated hydraulic conductivity, and that this effect extended down to the subsoil [N4-F4]. Compaction also shifts pore size distribution toward smaller pores and reduces unsaturated conductivity, which reduces the inflow into roots and can cause the plant to close stomata [N3-F3]. This creates a feedback loop in which reduced hydraulic conductivity limits water uptake, reducing stomatal conductance and carbon assimilation rate [N3-F3]. The evidence also notes that soil water retention and transport properties are altered in response to compaction, which affects soil water flow [N7-R4]. Overall, compaction reduces water availability by decreasing hydraulic conductivity, reducing pore size distribution, and altering the soil’s ability to transmit water to roots [N4-F4][N3-F3][N7-R4].

Nutrient uptake is constrained by water transport limitations because water movement is a prerequisite for nutrient uptake and for maintaining root function. The maize study found that compaction reduced root elongation and delayed leaf appearance rate, thereby decreasing shoot and root dry weights and leaf area, and that carbon assimilation was reduced in early growth stages [N3-F3]. It also notes that reduced leaf area and shoot biomass were observed in maize grown on compacted soil, and that reduced photosynthetic activity was attributed to a drop in stomatal conductance and a chemical message from stressed roots [N3-F3]. This shows that nutrient and carbon acquisition are not independent of water uptake: reduced water availability can limit stomatal opening, reduce photosynthesis, and ultimately reduce the plant’s ability to assimilate and partition carbon [N3-F3]. The meta-analysis further states that changes in soil pore structure and hydraulic properties can negatively affect water storage and transport, root growth, and nutrient availability [N4-F4].

## 10) Integrated conclusion
Soil compaction reduces crop yield by acting on root development, shoot development, and the physiological mechanisms that connect them. Compaction increases mechanical impedance, reduces root penetration, and alters root elongation, branching, and lateral root formation [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R5][N4-F4][N2-F2][N3-F3]. It also restricts root distribution depth and access to water and nutrients by reducing porosity, pore size distribution, and hydraulic conductivity [N4-F4][N3-F3]. Compaction indirectly affects shoot growth by constraining root exploration, reducing water and nutrient supply, and triggering physiological stress signals that lower carbon assimilation and photosynthetic activity [N3-R2][N3-F3][N2-F2]. Across major crops and soils, compaction reduces yield, with short-term effects often more pronounced than long-term effects [N4-F4][N1-F1]. Management practices such as conservation tillage can help mitigate yield loss, but compaction remains a persistent constraint on crop performance [N6-R3][N4-F4]. Root-soil hydraulic coupling explains how compaction constrains water and nutrient uptake by reducing hydraulic conductivity and altering the plant’s ability to move water from soil to shoot [N7-R1][N7-R5][N4-F4][N3-F3].

Overall, the evidence supports a single, integrated explanation: soil compaction reduces crop yield primarily by limiting root growth and function, which in turn limits shoot growth and the plant’s ability to acquire water and nutrients [N1-F1][N3-F3][N4-F4][N7-R1]. This makes compaction a mechanistic rather than merely an environmental constraint on yield [N2-F2][N4-F4].
